papers.title_in_file: Hybrid quantum-classical convolutional neural networks to improve molecular protein binding affinity predictions (arXiv:2301.06331v2, 18 Jan 2023, labelled VERSION #1)
papers.version_note: The text layer holds the paper twice (the second copy is a two-column rendering of the same text). The first copy was read in full; the second was used only to check quotes. The file is the paper the record names.

figures.shows: Three-panel pipeline picture: original protein-ligand pair (the 1br6 sample, protein ribbon with the drug biomolecule marked), then the voxelized feature-extraction grid (3D axes X, Y, Z, about 0 to 50 voxels), then the same grid after a Gaussian blur, which is denser. No numeric result.
figures.confirmed_by: The first step of the processing is the feature extraction, where 19 features are voxelized in a 3D space. Then, a Gaussian blur is applied to produce a dense representation of the data.

figures.shows: Top: generic 3D CNN schematic (convolutional layers with a skip connection, pooling layers, flattening and feed-forward layers). Bottom: the 3D CNN used, input then Conv 7x7x7x64 (three times, with two residual additions), Conv 7x7x7x128, pooling 2x2x2, Conv 5x5x5x256, pooling 2x2x2, flatten, FC 10, FC 1.
figures.confirmed_by: The network contains five 3D convolutional layers, with 64,64,64,128 and 256 filters respectively.

figures.shows: Hybrid architecture: the original data goes to a classical convolutional layer and, in parallel, a quantum convolutional layer (random quantum circuit, quantum filters). The two outputs are summed (aggregation node) and passed to the remaining convolutional, pooling, flattening and feed-forward layers.
figures.confirmed_by: The processed protein-ligand data is fed to both a classical and a quantum convolutional layer. The outputs are aggregated by using a residual connection and then fed to the subsequent classical convolutional and pooling layers.

figures.shows: FRQI scaling: block size n (x, 2 to 16) against number of qubits (left y, linear, 4 to about 13, red) and number of gates (right y, logarithmic, 10^2 to 10^5, blue). Qubits rise stepwise from 4 at n=2 to about 13 from n=14; gates track the same shape on the log axis, reaching about 10^5 at n=14 to 16.
figures.confirmed_by: Fig. 4 shows that the number of gates of a general FRQI encoding scales linearly with the dimension of the block, n3.

figures.shows: Four 3D voxel renderings (axes X, Y, Z, about 0 to 50): original data (blocky yellow volume) and the quantum-convolutional-layer output for circuits with 20, 100 and 1000 gates. The output is smoother and more spread as the gate count grows. No numeric values.
figures.confirmed_by: We see that with a low number of gates, the quantum layer extracts simpler quantum features than with a higher number of gates.

figures.shows: Validation metrics (RMSE, MAE, R2, Pearson, Spearman) against training epoch (x, 0 to 100) for the classical CNN (left panel) and the hybrid CNN with 300 gates (right panel). Left y-axis about -10 to 6, right y-axis 0.1 to 0.8. All curves are noisy for roughly the first 20 epochs then flat; a dashed vertical line marks epoch 50. Pearson and Spearman oscillate more than the others.
figures.confirmed_by: We see that for both cases, all the error metrics have stabilized after 50 epochs.

figures.shows: Test (core set) RMSE, MAE, Pearson, Spearman and R2 for Ising, 20, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 and 600 gate hybrids trained with the refined set, against a dashed classical baseline (RMSE about 1.6, MAE about 1.26, Pearson about 0.68, Spearman about 0.67, R2 about 0.46). 20 gates is worst (RMSE about 1.72, Pearson about 0.62). 300 to 600 gates are at or near the baseline; 500 gates is best (RMSE about 1.56, Pearson about 0.70).
figures.confirmed_by: The results show that, in general, the performance of the hybrid CNN models increases with the number of quantum gates until it reaches roughly the same performance as the classical CNN, at 300 quantum gates.

figures.shows: Same five metrics and models as Figure 7, trained with the general set. Classical baseline: RMSE about 1.6, MAE about 1.28, Pearson about 0.68, Spearman about 0.67, R2 about 0.46. 20 to 200 gates and Ising are worse than baseline; 300 to 500 gates reach or pass it; 600 gates has R2 about 0.437 (below baseline) and Pearson about 0.70.
figures.confirmed_by: The performance of the hybrid G3 models increases with the number of quantum gates until it converges at around 300 gates.

figures.shows: Quantum-circuit output probabilities (y, 0 to about 0.004) for the first 20 basis states (x, bit strings 000000000 to 000010011) under depolarizing, amplitude damping and phase damping noise, for p = 0 (black), 0.03, 0.008, 0.005, 0.003 and 0.001. The noiseless peak is about 0.0042. At p=0.03 the curves are nearly flat near about 0.001 (amplitude damping flat near about 0.0005 to 0.001); lower p curves approach the noiseless curve, and phase damping stays closest.
figures.confirmed_by: We see that the three noise models reduce the probability amplitude of the circuits' outputs.

figures.shows: Same 20 outputs at p = 0.01 for the three noise models: exact (black), noisy (blue) and error-mitigated (orange). Mitigated curves follow the exact curve closely for depolarizing and phase damping. For amplitude damping the mitigated curve takes negative values at several states (down to about -0.0013).
figures.confirmed_by: Even though the noise of the quantum device significantly reduces the amplitudes of the distribution, the DRER algorithm can recover the original amplitudes with significant accuracy.

figures.shows: Training time for hybrid and classical CNN and relative difference: Azure CPU 10.7 days against 18.3 days (42%); Azure GPU 24h against 39h (38%); Purdue Anvil GPU 16.3h against 22.1h (26%). Training parameters, all hardware: 8088499 against 10137129 (20%).
figures.confirmed_by: The improvement in training times with the hybrid model over the classical varies from 26% to 42%.

figures.shows: Hardware specification: Azure CPU is Intel Xeon E5-2673 v3 2.4 GHz, 4 cores, 14GB; Azure GPU is Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3, 6 cores, 1 x NVIDIA Tesla K80, 56GB; Purdue Anvil GPU is 2 x 3rd Gen AMD EPYC 7763, 128 cores, 4 x NVIDIA A100, 512GB.
figures.confirmed_by: In our experiments, the models have been trained using only CPUs and with two types of GPUs.

figures.shows: DRER error mitigation per noise model and error rate p (0.03, 0.01, 0.008, 0.005, 0.003, 0.001): regularization alpha, MSE of noisy circuits, MSE of mitigated circuits, tendency accuracy. Depolarizing tendency accuracy 0.59 to 0.89; amplitude damping 0.54 to 0.84; phase damping 0.67 to 0.85. At p=0.03 mitigated MSE is about equal to noisy MSE (9.7e-7 against 9.7e-7 for depolarizing).
figures.confirmed_by: Table III shows that when p ≤ 0.01 the MSE of the mitigated circuits is smaller than the MSE of the noisy circuits.

papers.what_it_is: A hybrid quantum-classical 3D CNN for protein-ligand binding affinity on PDBBind, whose first convolutional layer is a random-circuit quantum filter (FRQI encoding), compared with a classical CNN in simulation, plus a noisy-simulation test of data-regression error mitigation.

existing.note: The threshold is for the data regression error mitigation (DRER) algorithm, tested only in noisy simulation on the quantum convolutional layer with 300 gates (blocks of size 8, 9 qubits), on a small set of samples. The paper's own result sections state it for that circuit; the conclusion states it without that scope.
existing.value: The authors report that when the error rates are smaller than p = 0.01, the data regression error mitigation (DRER) algorithm can successfully mitigate the errors on the quantum convolutional layer with 300 gates; the noisy circuits were evaluated by simulation for a small set of samples.
existing.anchor: Section III, p.12; Section II.E, p.7; Section IV, p.13
quotes: All in all, these results show that as long as the error rates are smaller than p = 0.01, the DRER algorithm can successfully mitigate the errors introduced by the quantum device on the quantum convolutional layer with 300 gates.
we have also evaluated the performance of the noisy quantum circuits using three different noise models for a small set of samples.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.
existing.reader_inference: The stored value is the conclusion's wording; the paper's results section limits it to a 300-gate circuit and to simulated noise.

quotes: The performance of the models is evaluated against the core set of the 2020 PDBBind dataset.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its evaluation setup (Section III, p.8).

existing.note: The 20% is a reduction in training parameters (the paper's measure of complexity), 10137129 to 8088499 in Table I. Equal performance holds only from about 300 gates upward (Figure 7); hybrids with 20 to 200 gates and the Ising hybrid perform worse than the classical CNN. All quantum circuits were simulated.
existing.value: The authors report that the hybrid CNN has around 8 million training parameters against around 10 million for the classical CNN, a 20% reduction in model complexity, and that its performance reaches roughly the classical performance at 300 quantum gates.
quotes: The classical CNN has around 10 million parameters, while the hybrid CNNs have around 8 million parameters, proving a 20% reduction in model complexity.
the performance of the hybrid CNN models increases with the number of quantum gates until it reaches roughly the same performance as the classical CNN, at 300 quantum gates.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, in simulation.
existing.reader_inference: The abstract's phrase 'maintaining optimal performance' holds only for circuits with 300 or more gates.

existing.note: Table I gives 42%, 38% and 26% on three hardware types; the abstract's 'up to 40%' is rounded and the conclusion says 20%-40%. The paper also states that the hybrid model with PQCs trained longer than the classical CNN in its experiments; the savings are for the random-circuit (no trainable parameter) hybrid.
existing.value: The authors report that the improvement in training times of the hybrid model over the classical varies from 26% to 42% depending on hardware (Table I), and that the abstract states time savings of up to 40%.

papers.title_in_file: Taking advantage of noise in quantum reservoir computing (arXiv:2301.06814v3, 8 Jun 2023)
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv v3 (dated June 9, 2023), 8 PDF pages. The text layer holds the text twice (a second extraction of the same pages, interleaving columns); the first copy was read and the second used only to check quotes. The file is the paper the record names.

figures.shows: Mean squared error (y, log scale 1e-6 to 1e-3) of the quantum reservoir for the LiH task against number of gates (x, 25 to 900, categorical axis with 25 to 200 in steps and then 300, 500, 700, 900), in three panels (a amplitude damping, b depolarizing, c phase damping), one series per error probability p = 0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.003 and the noiseless p = 0 (black). Noiseless MSE rises to about 1e-4 near 55 gates, falls to about 1.4e-6 near 175 gates and stays about 2e-6 beyond. In panel a, p = 0.0005 lies below the noiseless curve from about 85 to about 135 gates; p = 0.003 lies above it for most gate counts. All noisy curves with p of 0.0005 or more rise at large gate counts, ending near 1e-3 for p = 0.003.

assertions.value: The authors state that an exact quadratization replaces each four-local term with one constant, four linear and six quadratic terms at the expense of two ancilla qubits per four-local term, giving a qubit overhead of O(n3) for LABS or O(n4) for H4full, which is impractical on current hardware.
quotes: an exact quadratization that exactly conserves the full structure of the HUBO replaces each fourlocal term with one constant, four linear, and six quadratic terms at the expense of adding two ancilla qubits

per four-local term [54]. This implies that implementing four-local Hamiltonians with O(n3) terms, such as LABS, or O(n4) terms, such as H4full, requires circuits with a qubit overhead scaling as O(n3) or O(n4), respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (Ref. 54).

assertions.value: The authors state that in the hypergraph clique expansion each hyperedge with k nodes generates a k-clique, and that the weight assigned to a pair of nodes shared by several hyperedges minimizes the sum of squared differences from the hyperedge weights, so the resulting edge weight is a weighted mean of the hyperedges it belongs to.
assertions.anchor: Section III.A, p.4; Appendix C, p.10
quotes: Therefore, each hyperedge e with k nodes in E generates a k-clique in G with edge-set E(e).
Therefore, the weight of the resulting edges is a weighted mean of the hyperedges it belongs to.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the method and its closed-form weights (Section III.A, p.4; Appendix C, p.10).

assertions.value: The authors state that the second quadratization method generates an Ansatz from a potentially fully quadratic Hamiltonian whose parameters theta are optimized simultaneously with the QAOA angles beta and gamma to minimize the energy of the original cost Hamiltonian, so the Ansatz Hamiltonian is a quadratization of the original quartic Hamiltonian.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quadratizations introduce an inconsistency between the cost operator and the Ansatz operator so the convergence guarantee of a typical QAOA in the limit p to infinity is lost and the approach is inherently heuristic, although for the H2'(theta) Ansatz convergence as p to infinity may still persist as long as it shares the same ground state as the cost Hamiltonian.
